title: For and Since
overview: This unit is about how long something has been true. You say it with for and since. You ask and answer How long questions. You also talk about a person or a place you do not name.
learningPath: Lesson: hear for and since inside an ordinary week.
Words: four groups, thirty-two words for time, homes and health.
Pattern 1: for a length of time, since a starting point.
Pattern 2: How long have you had it, and the short answer.
Reading: three texts, then nine questions with answers.
Speaking and writing: six spoken tasks and four short texts.
Quiz, then the assignment: say it and write it.
lectureScript:
Welcome to Unit 8.
This unit answers one question: how long?
Not when something happened. How long it has been true.
Look at these two sentences.
I have lived in this flat for three years.
I have lived in this flat since March.
Both sentences are about the same time.
After for comes a length of time.
Three years. Two weeks. Six months. A long time.
After since comes a starting point.
March. Monday. Last year. Nine o clock.
So ask yourself one thing.
Is this a length, or is it a start?
A length takes for. A start takes since.
Now look at the verb.
We do not say I live here for three years.
We say I have lived here for three years.
Have, then the past form.
It began before now, and it is still true now.
That is the whole idea of this unit.
The thing started in the past, and it has not stopped.
Here are more examples from an ordinary week.
She has worked at the shop since January.
They have had the same landlord for two years.
He has had a pain in his foot since the accident.
Nobody has used that room for a month.
Now the question.
How long have you lived here?
How long have you worked there?
How long have you had it?
The answer can be very short.
For three years. Since March. Not long.
You do not have to say a whole sentence back.
A short answer is normal and polite.
Listen to the question carefully.
How long asks about a length of time.
When asks about one point in the past.
When did you come here? Last year.
How long have you been here? For a year.
Same time, two questions, two different answers.
Now the third pattern.
Sometimes you do not know the person, or you do not want to name them.
Somebody has left a bag by the door.
Nobody has fixed the hot water yet.
Has anybody seen my key?
Everybody in the block knows about it.
Each of these words means one, so the verb is has.
We say nobody has, not nobody have.
The same thing happens with places.
Somewhere, anywhere, nowhere, everywhere.
I have looked everywhere for that paper.
It is nowhere in this room.
Nobody and nowhere already mean not.
So we do not add a second not.
We say nobody came. We do not say nobody did not come.
The words in this unit are for time, for a home and for health.
Period, phase, occasion, regular, constant, permanent, temporary, rarely.
Rent, landlord, tenant, deposit, contract, neighbourhood, flat, block.
Pain, symptom, treatment, medicine, prescription, recover, illness, injury.
The home words and the health words here are only examples.
They show you the English.
They are not advice about your own home or your own body.
In every task you may use a made-up name and a made-up address.
Now start with the words, then the three patterns.
Say every example out loud once before you write it.

outcomes.evidence: Pattern 2 practice, six items self-checked; Practice 3 six or more of eight; Speaking 3 recording of both parts.

words.meaning: A length of time with a start and an end.
words.example: I was away for a short period last year.
practice: The hot water was off for a period of two weeks.
She had a quiet period after the accident.
How long was that period?
A period of three months is not a long time.
words.starter: The busiest period of my day is ...
words.tutor: Ask me for three sentences that use period for a length of time, then one that uses it wrongly so I can find the mistake.

words.meaning: One part of a longer time, when things are one way.
words.example: The first phase of the work has finished.
practice: We are in the quiet phase of the year.
That was only a phase, and it is over now.
Which phase comes next?
The last phase took six weeks.
words.starter: One phase of my week is ...
words.tutor: Ask me the difference between a period and a phase, with one example of each.

words.meaning: A single time when something happens.
words.example: I have only been there on one occasion.
practice: On that occasion nobody was at home.
A wedding is a special occasion.
She has called the office on three occasions.
It rained on every occasion.
words.starter: I have been to a market on one occasion, and it was ...
words.tutor: Ask me to use occasion in three sentences: one about a single time, one about a special day and one in a question.

words.meaning: Happening again and again at the same times.
words.example: The bus is regular in the morning.
practice: She is a regular customer at the shop.
I have had regular work since April.
Is the pain regular, or does it come and go?
We have a regular class every Tuesday.
words.starter: One regular part of my week is ...
words.tutor: Ask me for two sentences with regular and two with rarely, so I can hear the difference.

words.meaning: Going on all the time, without stopping.
words.example: There was a constant sound from the street.
practice: The pain was constant for two days.
She needs constant help with the heavy boxes.
The hot water is not constant in this block.
Is the sound constant, or only at night?
words.starter: The most constant thing in my day is ...
words.tutor: Ask me whether constant and regular mean the same thing, and give me one example that shows they do not.

words.meaning: Lasting for ever, or for a very long time.
words.example: She has a permanent job at the hospital.
practice: The tree in front of the block looks permanent.
This is not a permanent address.
He has had a permanent home since last year.
Is the change permanent?
words.starter: One permanent thing in this neighbourhood is ...
words.tutor: Ask me for one permanent thing and one temporary thing inside the same short story.

words.meaning: Lasting only a short time.
words.example: The hot water is off, but this is temporary.
practice: I have a temporary contract for six months.
The shop has a temporary sign in the window.
Her pain was temporary and it has gone.
Is the work permanent or temporary?
words.starter: Something temporary in my week is ...
words.tutor: Ask me to say six sentences and to tell you which of them are about temporary things.

words.meaning: Not often. Only a few times.
words.example: I rarely go out on a Monday.
practice: She rarely sees the landlord.
We rarely have rain at this time of year.
He has rarely been ill since he was a child.
I rarely take medicine.
words.tutor: Ask me where rarely goes in a sentence, then give me three sentences with rarely in the wrong place to correct.

words.meaning: The money you pay every month to live in a place you do not own.
words.example: The rent is 40 a week.
practice: The rent has not changed since last April.
She pays the rent on the first day of the month.
How much is the rent?
The rent went up for a short period last year.
words.starter: The rent for a small flat here is about ...
words.tutor: Ask me for four sentences with rent, and make one of them a question about how much it is.

words.meaning: The person who owns a place and lets somebody live in it for money.
words.example: The landlord sent a man to fix the hot water.
practice: We have had the same landlord for two years.
Write to the landlord and keep a copy.
The landlord keeps the deposit until the end.
Who is the landlord of this block?
words.starter: A landlord is the person who ...
words.tutor: Take the part of a landlord and answer three questions about a flat, then swap and let me answer.

words.meaning: The person who pays rent and lives in a place they do not own.
words.example: She has been the tenant in flat 9 for four years.
practice: Every tenant in Block C got the same notice.
The tenant pays the rent and the landlord fixes the water.
How many tenants are there in this block?
He has been a good tenant since the first month.
words.starter: A tenant is a person who ...
words.tutor: Ask me the difference between a tenant and a landlord, with one sentence for each.

words.meaning: Money you pay at the start and get back at the end, if nothing is broken.
words.example: I paid a deposit before I got the key.
practice: The deposit was the same as one month of rent.
Ask about the deposit in writing.
She got her deposit back after two weeks.
How much is the deposit?
words.tutor: Ask me three questions a tenant might ask about a deposit, and answer each one for me.

words.meaning: A paper that two people sign, which says what each of them must do.
words.example: I signed the contract on the same day.
practice: The first contract was for one year.
Read the contract before you sign it.
My contract ends in September.
They have had the same contract since April.
words.tutor: Ask me for four sentences with contract: two about a flat and two about work.

words.meaning: The streets and buildings around the place where you live.
words.example: I like this neighbourhood.
practice: She has lived in this neighbourhood since she was young.
There is a market in the neighbourhood.
The neighbourhood is quiet at night.
Everybody in the neighbourhood knows that shop.
words.tutor: Ask me to describe a neighbourhood in five sentences, and use for or since in two of them.

words.meaning: A home of a few rooms, inside a larger building.
words.example: The flat is on the top floor.
practice: I have lived in this flat for three years.
There are twenty flats in Block C.
The flat has two rooms and a kitchen.
Which flat has the notice on the door?
words.tutor: Ask me the difference between a flat and a block, with one sentence for each.

words.meaning: A large building with many flats in it.
words.example: There are twenty flats in this block.
practice: Everybody in the block got the same notice.
The hot water in the block has been off since Monday.
She has lived in Block C for four years.
Which block do they live in?
words.starter: A block is a building with ...
words.tutor: Ask me for three sentences about a block of flats, using somebody, nobody and everybody.

words.meaning: The bad feeling in your body when something hurts.
words.example: He has had a pain in his foot since the accident.
practice: The pain was constant for two days.
She went to the doctor about the pain in her leg.
How long has she had the pain?
The pain is temporary and it will go.
words.starter: A pain is what you feel when ...
words.tutor: Ask me three How long questions about a pain in a story, and let me answer each one with for or since.

words.meaning: A sign in your body that shows something is wrong.
words.example: Pain is one symptom.
practice: A doctor asks about every symptom.
The first symptom was a very hot head.
She has had the same symptom for a week.
What was the first symptom?
words.starter: A symptom is something that shows ...
words.tutor: Ask me the difference between a symptom and an illness, with one example of each.

words.meaning: What a doctor or a nurse does to help somebody get better.
words.example: The treatment took six weeks.
practice: He has had the same treatment since March.
The treatment worked and she has recovered.
Every treatment is different.
How long does the treatment take?
words.tutor: Ask me for four sentences with treatment, and check that two of them use for or since.

words.meaning: Something you take to help you get better when you are ill.
words.example: He has taken that medicine for two weeks.
practice: The chemist had the medicine on the shelf.
She has not taken any medicine since Friday.
The medicine is in a small bottle.
How often does he take the medicine?
words.starter: Medicine is something you take when ...
words.tutor: Ask me to put medicine into three sentences: one with for, one with since and one question.

words.meaning: A paper from a doctor that lets you get medicine at the chemist.
words.example: The doctor wrote a prescription.
practice: Take the prescription to the chemist.
She has had the same prescription since January.
The prescription is for two weeks of medicine.
Where is the prescription?
words.starter: A prescription is a paper that ...
words.tutor: Ask me the difference between a prescription and medicine, with one sentence for each.

words.meaning: To get well again after an illness or an injury.
words.example: Some people recover in a few days.
practice: He has not recovered from the injury yet.
She recovered after a long period at home.
It takes time to recover.
How long did it take him to recover?
words.tutor: Ask me for four sentences with recover: two in the past and two with have or has.

words.meaning: The state of not being well inside your body.
words.example: An illness and an injury are not the same thing.
practice: He was away from work for a short illness.
The illness went on for two weeks.
Nobody in the block has had that illness.
Is the illness permanent or temporary?
words.tutor: Ask me to use illness and injury inside one short story of four sentences.

words.meaning: A hurt to your body that comes from an accident.
words.example: An injury is a hurt from an accident, like a cut or a broken foot.
practice: He has had the injury since the accident in May.
The injury was temporary and he has recovered.
An old injury can be permanent.
How did the injury happen?
words.tutor: Ask me three How long questions about an injury in a story, and let me answer with for or since.

words.meaning: One person, when you do not say who.
words.example: Somebody has left a bag by the door.
practice: Somebody called the office this morning.
I need somebody to help me carry this.
Somebody in the block has a key.
Did somebody see the notice?
words.tutor: Ask me for four sentences with somebody, and check that the verb after it is has and not have.

words.meaning: All the people in a group.
words.example: Everybody in the block has the same landlord.
practice: Everybody got the same notice.
She knows everybody in the neighbourhood.
Everybody has to pay the rent on the first.
Is everybody here?
words.tutor: Ask me whether everybody takes has or have, then give me three sentences to correct.

words.meaning: Not one person.
words.example: Nobody has fixed the hot water yet.
practice: Nobody came to the door.
Nobody in the block knows the new tenant.
Nobody has used that room for a month.
Why did nobody call?
words.tutor: Say five sentences with nobody and put a second not into one of them, so I can find it.

words.meaning: Any person at all. We use it in questions and after not.
words.example: Has anybody seen my key?
practice: I have not told anybody about the contract.
Does anybody live in flat 12?
Anybody can read the notice in the hall.
I did not see anybody in the street.
words.tutor: Ask me when to use anybody and when to use somebody, with one example of each.

words.meaning: In one place, when you do not say where.
words.example: The notice is somewhere on this wall.
practice: I put the prescription somewhere safe.
She lives somewhere in this neighbourhood.
The shop was shut, so we went somewhere else.
It must be somewhere in this room.
words.tutor: Ask me for three sentences with somewhere, and one with somewhere else.

words.meaning: In any place at all. We use it in questions and after not.
words.example: I cannot find it anywhere.
practice: Have you seen it anywhere?
You can sit anywhere in this room.
I did not go anywhere last weekend.
Is there a chemist anywhere near here?
words.tutor: Ask me when to use anywhere and when to use somewhere, with one example of each.

words.meaning: In no place. Not in any place.
words.example: It is nowhere in this room.
practice: The notice was nowhere on the wall.
We looked in three shops and found it nowhere.
There is nowhere to put these boxes.
Nowhere in the block is quiet in the morning.
words.tutor: Ask me why we do not say it is not nowhere, then give me two sentences to correct.

words.meaning: In all places.
words.example: I have looked everywhere for that paper.
practice: There was water everywhere after the rain.
She has been everywhere in this neighbourhood.
Everywhere in the block was quiet.
I have carried this bag everywhere for years.
words.tutor: Ask me for four sentences with everywhere and nowhere, two of each.

grammar.title: Since Monday, For Two Weeks
grammar.explanation: Use for with a length of time: for two weeks, for three years. Use since with the point where it started: since Monday, since March. The verb is have or has plus the past form. It began before now, and it is still true now.
grammar.rule:
for, then a length of time
I have lived here for three years.
She has worked there for six months.
We have had this contract for a week.

since, then a starting point
I have lived here since March.
She has worked there since January.
We have had this contract since Monday.

the verb: have or has, then the past form
I have, you have, we have, they have
he has, she has, it has
lived, worked, had, been, taken, known

not the everyday present form
Wrong: I know him for a year.
Right: I have known him for a year.

a whole part of a sentence can be a starting point
I have lived here since I came to this street.
grammar.workedExample:
Here is one done for you.
The facts: I started this job in April. I am still there.
Step 1. Is April a length or a start? It is a start.
Step 2. A start takes since.
Step 3. The verb is have plus the past form: have worked.
Answer: I have worked here since April.
Now say the same thing with for.
April until now is six months.
Answer: I have worked here for six months.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to use the everyday present form here: I live here since March. English needs have or has plus the past form: I have lived here since March.
grammar.tip: For measures the gap. Since names the start.
grammar.practice:
Write for or since in each gap.
1. I have had this bag ... two years.
2. She has been our neighbour ... last April.
3. They have had no hot water ... Monday.
4. He has had a pain in his foot ... six days.
5. Nobody has used that flat ... a long time.
6. We have had the same landlord ... we came here.
7. The shop has been open ... nine o clock.
8. Now write two sentences of your own, one with for and one with since.
grammar.answers:
1. for  2. since  3. since  4. for  5. for  6. since  7. since
Item 8 is your own writing, so there is no fixed answer. Models: I have had this phone for a year. I have lived in this neighbourhood since January.
The likeliest wrong answer is item 6. We came here is a starting point, even though it is a whole part of a sentence and not a date. If you can put the word when in front of it, it is a start, so it takes since.

grammar.title: How Long Have You Had It?
grammar.explanation: How long asks about a length of time. Put how long first, then have or has, then the person. How long have you lived here? The answer can be short: for three years, or since March.
grammar.rule:
how long, then have or has, then the person, then the past form
How long have you lived here?
How long has she worked there?
How long have they had the flat?

short answers
For three years.
Since March.
Not long.
About a month.

a full answer repeats the verb
I have lived here for three years.
She has worked there since March.

how long is not the same as when
When did you come here? Last year.
How long have you been here? For a year.

he, she and it take has
How long has he taken that medicine?
grammar.workedExample:
Here is one done for you.
You want to ask about a person job. The person is she.
Step 1. Start with how long.
Step 2. Add have or has. She takes has.
Step 3. Add the person, then the past form: worked.
Question: How long has she worked there?
Step 4. Answer it two ways.
Short answer: Since January.
Full answer: She has worked there since January.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to use did in this question: How long did you live here? That asks about a finished time. For something that is still true, use have: How long have you lived here?
grammar.tip: How long asks about the gap. When asks about the point.
grammar.practice:
Write the question. Use how long.
1. You want to know about a person flat. (you)
2. You want to know about her job. (she)
3. You want to know about their contract. (they)
4. You want to know about his medicine. (he)
Now write a short answer for two of them.
5. Answer question 1 with a length of time.
6. Answer question 2 with a starting point.
grammar.answers:
1. How long have you lived in your flat?  2. How long has she worked there?  3. How long have they had the contract?  4. How long has he taken that medicine?
5. Model: For two years.  6. Model: Since January.
The likeliest wrong answers are items 2 and 4. With he and she the word is has, not have: How long has she worked there?

grammar.title: Somebody, Nobody, Everywhere
grammar.explanation: Use these words when you do not name the person or the place. Somebody, everybody, nobody and anybody are people. Somewhere, anywhere, nowhere and everywhere are places. Each one means one, so the verb is has, not have.
grammar.rule:
people
somebody, anybody: one person, and you do not say who
everybody: all the people
nobody: not one person

places
somewhere, anywhere: one place, and you do not say where
everywhere: all places
nowhere: not one place

the verb is has, not have
Somebody has left a bag by the door.
Nobody has fixed the hot water yet.
Everybody in the block has the same landlord.

anybody and anywhere go in questions and after not
Has anybody seen my key?
I cannot find it anywhere.

nobody and nowhere already mean not
Nobody came. We do not say nobody did not come.
grammar.workedExample:
Here is one done for you.
You want to say that not one person has fixed the hot water.
Step 1. Choose the word for not one person: nobody.
Step 2. Nobody already means not, so do not add a second not.
Step 3. The verb is has, not have.
Answer: Nobody has fixed the hot water.
Now ask the same thing as a question.
In a question the word is anybody.
Answer: Has anybody fixed the hot water?
grammar.mistake: It is easy to add a second not: Nobody did not answer the door. Nobody already means not one person, so one not is enough: Nobody answered the door.
grammar.tip: Nobody and nowhere carry the not inside them. One not is enough.
grammar.practice:
Choose the right word.
1. (Somebody, Nobody) has left a bag by the door. It is not mine.
2. I have looked (everywhere, nowhere) for my key and I cannot find it.
3. Has (anybody, nobody) seen the notice in the hall?
4. (Everybody, Anybody) in the block pays rent on the first of the month.
5. The shop was shut, so we went (somewhere, nowhere) else.
6. Nobody (has, have) told the landlord about the hot water.
grammar.answers:
1. Somebody  2. everywhere  3. anybody  4. Everybody  5. somewhere  6. has
The likeliest wrong answer is item 6. Nobody means one person, so the verb is has: Nobody has told the landlord.
Item 2 is the next one people miss. The sentence already has cannot, but looked is not after it, so the word here is everywhere.

readings.title: Three Years in Block C
readings.setting: A flat on the top floor of a block of flats
readings.passage:
My name is Yara, and I have lived in this flat for three years.
It is on the top floor of Block C.
I am the tenant, and the person who owns the flat is my landlord.
When I came here, I paid a deposit and signed a contract.
The first contract was for one year.
I have signed a new one twice since then.
The rent is 40 a week, and it has not changed since last April.
I like this neighbourhood.
The shop on the corner has been open since before I came.
The woman there has worked in it for eleven years, and she knows everybody.
Last year there was no hot water in Block C.
It was cold for a week in January, and again in February.
For a long time nobody could fix it.
Then the landlord sent a man with the right tools.
The water has been hot since March.
Some things here are temporary and some are permanent.
My contract is temporary, because it ends in September.
The old tree in front of the block feels permanent.
It has stood there for fifty years.
I do not know where I will live next year.
But I have been happy here for three years.
In one flat, that is a long time.

readings.title: Getting Better Takes Time
readings.setting: A general information page, not about any one person
readings.passage:
This page is an example of general information.
It is not advice about any one person.
An illness and an injury are not the same thing.
An illness is when your body is not well inside.
An injury is a hurt from an accident, like a cut or a broken foot.
Both of them take time.
A doctor asks two questions very often.
What is the symptom? How long have you had it?
A symptom is a sign that something is wrong.
Pain is one symptom. Feeling tired all day is another.
The answer to how long matters.
A pain for two days and a pain for two months are not the same.
That is why a doctor writes down the day it started.
Treatment is what a doctor or a nurse does to help.
Sometimes the treatment is medicine.
A doctor can write a prescription.
A prescription is a paper that lets you get that medicine at the chemist.
Some people recover in a few days.
Others need a longer period.
A cut on the leg is usually temporary.
An old injury can be permanent, and the person learns to live with it.
Everybody is different, so nobody can say how long one person will take.
Only a doctor can answer that question for one person.
This text is here to show you the English words, and nothing more.

readings.title: Notice in the Hall of Block C
readings.setting: The wall inside the front door of a block of flats
readings.passage:
BLOCK C: NOTICE TO ALL TENANTS
Written on 14 March. Please read it all.

HOT WATER
The hot water has been off in flats 12 to 20 since Monday 10 March.
We are sorry. This is temporary.
A man has come twice to fix it.
He comes back on Friday 21 March with the right tool.
The water will be hot again the same day.

THE FRONT DOOR
The front door has been slow to close since January.
Do not leave it open.
If you see it open, please close it.

RENT
You pay the rent on the first day of every month.
The rent has not changed since last April, and it will not change this year.
If your contract ends in the next three months, the office will send you a note.

THE BINS
The men empty the bins every Tuesday morning.
Somebody has left boxes beside the bins.
Please do not leave boxes there.
There is no room, and the men cannot carry them.

WHO TO CALL
For the hot water, the door or the bins, call the office on 555 0199.
The office is open from 9 in the morning until 5 in the afternoon, Monday to Friday.
For anything about your contract or your deposit, write to the office and keep a copy.

The landlord office, Block C

comprehension.q: How long has Yara lived in the flat?
comprehension.why: The first line says she has lived there for three years. Three years is a length of time, so it takes for.

comprehension.q: What two things did Yara do when she came to the flat?
comprehension.a: She paid a deposit and signed a contract.
comprehension.why: One line says she paid a deposit and signed a contract on the day she came.

comprehension.q: In this text, who is the landlord?
comprehension.a: The person who owns the flat.
comprehension.why: Yara says she is the tenant, and the person who owns the flat is her landlord.

comprehension.q: Why does Yara call her contract temporary?
comprehension.a: Because it ends in September, so it will not last.
comprehension.why: Temporary means lasting only a short time. She says the contract ends in September.

comprehension.q: What are the two questions the text says a doctor asks very often?
comprehension.a: What is the symptom, and how long have you had it?
comprehension.why: Both questions are printed one after the other, just after the line about a doctor.

comprehension.q: In this text, what is a prescription?
comprehension.a: A paper that lets you get medicine at the chemist.
comprehension.why: The text gives the meaning in the line straight after it names the word.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say nobody can tell you how long one person will take?
comprehension.a: Because everybody is different, so only a doctor can answer for one person.
comprehension.why: The text gives the reason in the same line: everybody is different. It then says a doctor answers for one person.

comprehension.q: You live in flat 15 and you have no hot water. What day will it be hot again?
comprehension.why: The notice says the man comes back on Friday 21 March. It also says the water will be hot the same day.

comprehension.q: Your contract ends next month and you want to ask about your deposit. What does the notice tell you to do?
comprehension.a: Write to the office and keep a copy.
comprehension.why: The last part says to write to the office about a contract or a deposit. It also says to keep a copy. The phone number is for the hot water, the door or the bins.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — For or Since
speaking.instructions:
Say each line out loud. Then record all six and play them back.
1. I have lived here for three years.
2. I have lived here since March.
3. She has worked there for six months.
4. She has worked there since January.
5. They have had the contract for a week.
6. They have had the contract since Monday.
Check yourself. After for you say a length of time.
After since you say a starting point.
If you cannot hear the difference, say lines 1 and 2 again, slowly.
speaking.tutor: Say six for and since sentences about a flat, and stop after each one so I can repeat it.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Listen to the Question, Then Answer
speaking.instructions:
Listen to each question. Then say your answer out loud.
1. How long have you lived in your home?
2. How long have you studied English?
3. How long have you had your phone?
4. When did you start studying English?
5. How long has your neighbour lived there?
One of these questions is not the same kind as the others.
Question 4 asks when, so the answer is a point in the past.
The other four ask how long, so the answer takes for or since.
Made-up answers are fine for all five.
Record yourself and play it back. Count how many answers begin with for or since.
speaking.tutor: Read me one How long question and one When question, one after the other, and let me answer both before you say which was which.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Ask and Answer
speaking.instructions:
This drill has two parts and you take both of them.
Ask the question, wait two seconds, then answer it.
1. How long have you lived in this neighbourhood? Then: For two years.
2. How long have you had that contract? Then: Since April.
3. How long has the hot water been off? Then: Since Monday.
Now do the same with three questions and answers of your own.
Record both parts and play them back.
Check yourself. Every question starts with how long, then have or has.
If somebody is with you, you can ask them instead and answer their question back.
speaking.tutor: Take the part of a neighbour. Ask me how long I have lived here, then answer when I ask you the same question.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Talk About a Home
speaking.instructions:
Talk for one minute about a home. It does not have to be yours.
You may invent the tenant, the flat and the address.
Use these five ideas in this order.
1. Who lives there, and how long they have lived there.
2. The neighbourhood, and one thing in it.
3. The rent, and if it has changed.
4. One thing that is temporary.
5. One thing that is permanent.
Record yourself and play it back.
Check yourself. Count your for and since sentences. Three or more is good.
speaking.tutor: Listen to my one-minute talk about a flat, and tell me only if I used for and since correctly.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Somebody, Nobody, Everywhere
speaking.instructions:
Say each sentence out loud twice.
1. Somebody has left a bag by the door.
2. Nobody has fixed the hot water yet.
3. Has anybody seen the notice in the hall?
4. Everybody in the block pays the rent on the first.
5. I have looked everywhere for that paper.
6. It is nowhere in this room.
Record yourself and play it back.
Check yourself. In lines 1, 2 and 4 you must hear has, not have.
Line 2 has the word nobody and no second not.
speaking.tutor: Give me five sentences with somebody, nobody, anybody and everybody, and tell me if I say have where has belongs.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — How Long, in Your Own Words
speaking.instructions:
Speak for ninety seconds. You may use made-up facts for all of it.
Say five things that have been true for a long time.
One about a place. One about work or study.
One about a person you know. One about a thing you own.
One about a neighbourhood.
Every sentence uses have or has plus the past form, with for or since.
Record yourself and play it back.
Check yourself with this list. Five sentences. Five different subjects.
Three uses of for. Two uses of since.
speaking.tutor: After my ninety-second talk, ask me one How long question about something I said.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Five Sentences About a Home
writing.prompt:
Write five sentences about a home.
You may invent the tenant, the flat and the address.
Use for in two sentences and since in two sentences.
One sentence uses the word neighbourhood.
writing.model:
Ana has lived in flat 9 for four years.
She has been the tenant since April.
She paid a deposit and signed a contract on the same day.
The rent has not changed for two years.
She knows everybody in the neighbourhood.
writing.starter: Ana has lived in flat ... for ...
writing.criteria: Five sentences. Two with for. Two with since. One with the word neighbourhood. Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.
writing.support: Write the two for sentences first. Copy the shape from the model: person, has lived, for, length of time.
writing.extension: Add a sixth sentence that names one temporary thing and one permanent thing in the same home.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Answer Four How Long Questions
writing.prompt:
Write a full answer to each question. Made-up answers are fine.
1. How long have you lived in your home?
2. How long have you studied English?
3. How long have you had your phone?
4. How long have you known your oldest friend?
Each answer is one full sentence, not a short answer.
writing.model:
I have lived in my home for two years.
I have studied English since last September.
I have had my phone for eleven months.
I have known my oldest friend since we were at school.
writing.starter: I have lived in my home for ...
writing.criteria: Four sentences. Each one has have or has plus the past form. Two use for and two use since.
writing.support: Answer question 1 out loud first, then write down exactly what you said.
writing.extension: Now write the four questions as well, each one above its own answer.

writing.title: Writing 3 — A Short Notice
writing.prompt:
Write a short notice for a block of flats. Invent everything in it.
It has a heading and four lines.
Say what is broken and how long it has been broken.
Then say what is happening and who to call.
writing.model:
BLOCK D: NOTICE TO ALL TENANTS
The front door has been slow to close since Monday.
A man is coming on Thursday to fix it.
This is temporary, so please do not leave the door open.
For the door, call the office on 555 0143.
writing.criteria: A heading in capital letters. Four lines under it. One line uses since or for. One line says who to call.
writing.support: Copy the heading from the model and change only the letter of the block. Then write the since line second.
writing.extension: Add one more line about the bins, using somebody or nobody.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Somebody, Nobody, Everywhere
writing.prompt:
Write six sentences about a block of flats that you invent.
Use somebody, nobody, anybody, everybody, everywhere and nowhere.
Use one of them in each sentence. Do not name any person.
writing.model:
Somebody has left a box beside the bins.
Nobody has come to take it for a week.
Has anybody asked the office about it?
Everybody in Block D walks past it every morning.
I have looked everywhere for the notice about the bins.
It is nowhere on this wall.
writing.criteria: Six sentences. Six different words from the list. After somebody, nobody, anybody and everybody the verb is has, not have.
writing.support: Write the nobody sentence first. Check that there is only one not word in it.
writing.extension: Turn two of your six sentences into questions with anybody or anywhere.

activities.title: Practice 1 — For or Since
activities.instructions:
Write for or since in each gap.
1. I have had this bag ... two years.
2. She has been our neighbour ... last April.
3. They have had no hot water ... Monday.
4. He has had a pain in his foot ... six days.
5. Nobody has used that flat ... a long time.
6. We have had the same landlord ... we came here.
7. The shop has been open ... nine o clock.
8. I have not seen anybody ... three days.
activities.answers:
1. for  2. since  3. since  4. for  5. for  6. since  7. since  8. for
Eight out of eight means you have it.
Six or seven means check the two you missed. Ask one question of each gap: is it a length, or is it a start?
Five or fewer means read Pattern 1 again before you go on.
activities.solo: Do it in writing, then read each finished sentence out loud. Your ear will catch a wrong one that your eye missed.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Put the Verb Right
activities.instructions:
Each sentence uses the wrong verb form.
Write it again with have or has plus the past form.
1. I live in this flat since March.
2. She works at the shop for six months.
3. They have no hot water since Monday.
4. He takes that medicine for two weeks.
5. We know our landlord since last year.
6. Nobody uses that room for a month.
activities.answers:
1. I have lived in this flat since March.
2. She has worked at the shop for six months.
3. They have had no hot water since Monday.
4. He has taken that medicine for two weeks.
5. We have known our landlord since last year.
6. Nobody has used that room for a month.
Items 3 and 5 are the hardest. The past form of have is had, and the past form of know is known.
Six out of six is a pass. Four or five means write the six past forms in a list and learn them.
activities.solo: Cover the answers with your hand. Write all six, then move your hand and mark them yourself.

activities.title: Practice 3 — How Long, or When?
activities.instructions:
Read each answer.
Write H if the question was How long. Write W if the question was When.
1. For three years.
2. Last April.
3. Since Monday.
4. In 2019.
5. For about a month.
6. Two weeks ago.
7. Since I came here.
8. On the first of May.
activities.answers:
1. H  2. W  3. H  4. W  5. H  6. W  7. H  8. W
Every answer with for or since belongs to How long. Every answer that names one point in the past belongs to When.
Item 7 is the one people miss. Since I came here names a start, so the question was How long.
Seven or eight is a pass.
activities.solo: After you mark it, say out loud the How long question that each H answer belongs to.

activities.title: Practice 4 — The Words of This Unit
activities.instructions:
Match each word to its meaning. Write the number and the letter.
1. tenant
2. deposit
3. temporary
4. constant
5. symptom
6. prescription
7. rarely
8. occasion
a. money you pay first and get back later
b. not often
c. a single time when something happens
d. going on all the time, without stopping
e. the person who pays rent and lives in a place
f. lasting only a short time
g. a sign in your body that something is wrong
h. a paper from a doctor that lets you get medicine
activities.answers:
1e  2a  3f  4d  5g  6h  7b  8c
Eight out of eight is a pass.
The pair people swap is 3 and 4. Temporary is about how long a thing lasts. Constant is about a thing that never stops.
Seven or fewer means read the word cards again, then try it a second time.
activities.solo: Cover the letters with a piece of paper. Say each meaning from memory first, then move the paper and check.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Nobody, Anybody, Everywhere
activities.instructions:
Choose the right word for each gap.
1. (Somebody, Anybody) has left a box beside the bins.
2. Has (anybody, nobody) called the office?
3. I have looked (everywhere, nowhere) and I still cannot find it.
4. (Everybody, Anybody) in Block C pays the rent on the first.
5. The notice is (somewhere, nowhere) on this wall, but I cannot see it.
6. Nobody (has, have) fixed the hot water yet.
7. We went to three shops and found it (nowhere, somewhere).
8. I have not told (anybody, nobody) about the contract.
activities.answers:
1. Somebody  2. anybody  3. everywhere  4. Everybody  5. somewhere  6. has  7. nowhere  8. anybody
Item 8 is the one people miss. The sentence already has not, so the word after it is anybody: I have not told anybody.
Eight out of eight is a pass. Six or seven means read Pattern 3 again.
activities.solo: Read each finished sentence out loud. A second not sounds wrong even before you can name the rule.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Find It in the Notice
activities.instructions:
Read the notice in the hall of Block C again.
Find the answer to each question and write which section it is in.
1. Since when has the hot water been off?
2. What day does the man come back?
3. How often do the men empty the bins?
4. What has been slow to close since January?
5. When did the rent last change?
6. What must you do if you want to ask about your deposit?
activities.answers:
1. Since Monday 10 March, under HOT WATER.
2. Friday 21 March, under HOT WATER.
3. Every Tuesday morning, under THE BINS.
4. The front door, under THE FRONT DOOR.
5. Last April, under RENT.
6. Write to the office and keep a copy, under WHO TO CALL.
Six out of six is a pass. Item 5 is the one people miss, because the notice says the rent has not changed since last April. That means April was the last change.
Four or five means read the notice one section at a time.
activities.solo: Put your finger on the heading of each section before you look for the answer. The headings tell you where to look.

options: I have lived here since March.
I have lived here since three years.
I am living here since March.
quizzes.a: I have lived here since March.
quizzes.why: Have plus the past form shows it began before now and is still true. Since names a starting point, and March is a point. I live here since March uses the wrong verb form. Since three years puts a length after since, and a length needs for.

quizzes.q: Choose the right word: She has worked at the chemist ... eight months.
quizzes.why: Eight months is a length of time, so it takes for. Since needs a starting point, like last April. From and ago do not go with this verb form here.

quizzes.q: Choose the right word: They have had the same landlord ... last September.
quizzes.why: Last September is the point where the time started, so it takes since. For needs a length, like two years. During and while go with a whole event, not with a starting point.

quizzes.q: Which question asks how long something has been true?
options: Did you live here last year?
How long have you lived here?
quizzes.a: How long have you lived here?
quizzes.why: How long asks about the length of time up to now, so the verb is have lived. When did you come here asks about one point in the past. The other two ask about place and about a finished year.

quizzes.q: Choose the best answer to this question: How long has she had that contract?
quizzes.why: How long takes for or since in the answer. Since January names the start, so it fits. She had it last year answers when, not how long. Yes she has answers a yes or no question, and this is not one.

options: How long has he taken that medicine?
How long have he taken that medicine?
How long he has taken that medicine?
How long did he take that medicine, and still now?
quizzes.a: How long has he taken that medicine?
quizzes.why: With he, she and it the word is has, not have. In a question the has comes before the person: has he taken. Option three leaves has after he, which is the order for a statement. Option four uses did, which asks about a finished time.
Nobody means one person, so the verb is has. Nobody already means not, so a second not is wrong. That rules out options two and three. Option one uses have, which goes with I, you, we and they.

quizzes.q: Choose the right word: I have not told ... about the contract.
quizzes.why: The sentence already has not, so the word after it is anybody. Nobody would put a second not into the same sentence. Everybody turns the meaning into the opposite. Nowhere is a word for a place, not for a person.

quizzes.q: Choose the right word: I have looked ... and I still cannot find it.
quizzes.why: Everywhere means in all places, which fits looking and not finding. Somewhere means one place, so it does not explain the long search. Nobody and anybody are words for people, not for places.

quizzes.q: In the notice for Block C, since when has the hot water been off?
quizzes.why: The hot water line gives that day. Friday 21 March is the day the man comes back. Last April is about the rent, and January is about the front door.

quizzes.q: Which word means lasting only a short time?
quizzes.why: Temporary means it does not last. Permanent is the opposite, because it lasts for a very long time. Constant means it never stops, which is about all the time. Regular means it happens again and again at the same times.

quizzes.q: Which word means a paper from a doctor that lets you get medicine?
quizzes.why: A prescription is the paper itself. A symptom is a sign in your body that something is wrong. Treatment is what a doctor or a nurse does to help. An injury is a hurt that comes from an accident.

teacherNotes.note: The commonest error at this stage is the everyday present form with since: I live here since March. It is not a vocabulary problem. The learner has the words and has chosen a form that feels natural for something that is still true. Do not correct it by naming a tense. Ask the learner to point at the two words have and lived in the model line, then to point at the same two places in their own sentence. The gap becomes visible without any grammar term.

Speaking 2 separates How long from When, and that separation is a listening skill before it is a grammar one. If the learner answers a When question with for a year, the difficulty is in the hearing, not in the forms. Read the two questions again, slowly, one after the other, and ask which one contains the words how long. Only then go back to the answers.

The home words and the health words in this unit are examples of English, never advice. No task asks the learner to describe their own housing, their own health or their own money, and every personal task states that a made-up answer is fine. Reading 2 says in its own first two lines that it is general information and not advice about any one person. If a learner volunteers a real situation, keep the work on the English and do not offer an opinion about the situation itself.

Pattern 1 item 6 and Practice 3 item 7 turn on the same point: a whole part of a sentence can be a starting point. Since we came here and since I came here take since exactly as since March does. The quickest test is whether the word when can go in front of the phrase. If it can, it is a start, so it takes since.

A learner who finishes early can redo Writing 4 with the place words only, or turn Speaking 6 into a set of six How long questions for the tutor to answer. A learner who is struggling should do Pattern 1 and Practice 1 twice on two different days rather than moving on. Eight correct gaps on the second day is worth more than six on the first.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say how long something has been true, using for and since.
I can understand a How long question when I hear it, and answer it.
I can ask somebody how long, and answer the same question back.
I can say four or five sentences about how long things have been true.
I can find the exact detail I need in a short text or a notice.
I can write five sentences with for and since, and check my spelling.
I can use somebody, nobody, anybody and everywhere correctly.

assignment.title: How Long: a spoken answer and a written notice
assignment.instructions:
This assignment has two parts. You may invent every fact in it.

Part 1, spoken.
Record ninety seconds about a home and the person who lives in it.
Say how long each thing has been true.
Use for at least three times and since at least twice.

Part 2, written.
Write a short notice for that block of flats.
Give it a heading in capital letters and four lines under it.
One line says what is broken and how long it has been broken.
One line uses somebody or nobody.
One line says who to call.

Before you send it, play your recording back once and read your notice out loud.
Fix anything you hear that is wrong.
assignment.submissionType: Audio recording and a written notice
